correctness.rationale: Writing x=Re1 and y=rv with c=<e1,v>, direct differentiation gives D_phi(x,y)=A(r)+R h_prime(r)(1-c), A(r)=h(R)-h(r)-h_prime(r)(R-r). The supporting-line inequality yields 0<=A(r)<=h(R)-h(r)->0. In dimension one every interior boundary approach is eventually radial and D->0. If h_prime is bounded, the gradient norm is bounded and D->0 for any approach in every dimension. In dimensions >=2 and h_prime->infinity, for any a>=0 choose c=1-a/(R h_prime) to obtain D=A+a; for divergent limit choose c=1-1/sqrt(h_prime), which gives D=A+R sqrt(h_prime)->infinity. Both cosine choices are admissible and yield y->x. The bounded-domain sublevel condition is automatic because y lies in the ball. Independent concrete Hellinger-style and quadratic radial identities were verified, not taken as a universal numerical proof.
residual_risks: Hypotheses demand h continuous finite at R and C1 radial on [0,R), h_prime(0)=0; no barrier kernels with infinite boundary values or arbitrary nonradial domains.

value.rationale: The classification answers a natural analytic kernel-eligibility question: under finite closed-ball boundary values, whether every interior approach has vanishing Bregman divergence. It identifies the exact radial steepness/dimension threshold and not just a negative example; the full continuum of attainable boundary defects reveals the magnitude and geometry of failure.
